title: How To Identify A Bully
author: Michael Linsin
summary: As a follow-up to an earlier comprehensive anti-bullying guide, Linsin addresses a specific gap: many victims aren't sure if they're actually being bullied, since bullies are often skilled at blending teasing with apparent friendliness. Rather than relying on students to distinguish bullying from ordinary friend conflict on their own, he proposes a simple, near-universal test: the victim directly and specifically asks the other student to stop a named behavior ("please stop tripping me"). If the person doesn't stop, Linsin argues, they are by definition a bully. He notes this doesn't replace teacher intervention against determined bullies, but it does give victims a concrete tool for clarity, puts potential bullies on notice that their motives can be tested, and can help borderline offenders recognize their own behavior as bullying once "please stop" becomes established classroom culture.
points: Many bullying victims are genuinely unsure whether they're being bullied, since bullies often mix mistreatment with apparent friendliness.
Proposed test: the victim specifically asks the other student to stop a named behavior — if they don't stop, they are by definition a bully.
This test doesn't replace teacher intervention against a determined bully but gives victims clarity and a concrete tool.
Making "please stop" a known classroom culture puts all potential bullies on notice and helps borderline offenders recognize their own behavior.
quotes: It is this: Many victims are unsure if they’re actually being bullied.
You see, bullies are good at making you think that they’re really your friend.
This underscores the importance of defining for your students—through modeling, playacting, and role-playing—what bullying looks like.
It’s a very simple test, but it’s 100% accurate in determining who is and isn’t a bully.
But what it does do is give the victim a surefire way to know if they’re being bullied. Because, if the person being asked doesn’t stop, then by definition, they’re a bully.
Furthermore, when “please stop” becomes the culture of your classroom or school it can virtually wipe out bullying behavior.
